How to read this screen — and the colour code

Click anywhere on a card to tick it; ticks are saved in this browser. The top bar shows the real time and which block the timetable says you should be in (it turns red when you are behind). → Now jumps to that block. Rehearse lets you pretend it is another time of day while practising tonight.

SAY — spoken. Read the big quoted text in your own voice.
SAY — TRANSITION — spoken. The line that moves you to the next block.
SAY — ANSWER — spoken, but only after delegates have tried.
ASK THE ROOM — pose the question, then stay quiet.
WAIT — press the timer button. Never read this card.

DO — a physical action: walk, count hands, help.

NOTE — for you only.

2A-2 · Revisions, revision numbers, timestamp and author

10:27–10:37 (10 min) · Slide 4 · Notes A2–A3 · LO 1–4
Goal: define revision control and name the two components of a revision (timestamp and author).
Show → Slide 4not spoken

The photo album: a drawing photographed four times, each photo with a note on the back.

Say

Here is how I would explain it to a six-year-old. You draw a picture of a house and put it on the fridge. Every time you change the drawing — add a tree, colour the roof — Mom takes a photo and writes on the back: number 3, Saturday 10 o'clock, Lerato, added a tree.

Now you can always go back. You can see what the house looked like before the tree. And you know who added the tree and when.

Say

That is all revision control is. A revision is one saved, changed state of a document or program. The revision number tells revisions apart: 1, 2, 3. And the curriculum says every revision has two main components: the timestamp, which answers when, and the author, which answers who. Good systems add a third thing: a short message that answers why.

Ask the roomnot spoken
Where have you already used revision control in your own life, without calling it that?
Waitnot spoken

Take three answers. Expect: Google Docs or Word version history, track changes, Moodle/LMS resubmissions, WhatsApp edited messages, bank statements.

Say

Exactly. Now why do we need a logical way to organise revisions in software? Three reasons. One: programs change all the time, often by more than one person. Two: when something breaks, you need to go back to the last version that worked. Three, and this is the one for us as lecturers: evidence. Who wrote this, when, and how did it grow? That is moderation, that is plagiarism checking, that is a portfolio of evidence.

Say — transition

Let's test that on a real mess.

2A-3 · Activity A: Folder chaos (session problem)

10:37–10:49 (12 min) · Slide 5 · Notes Activity A · pairs at neighbouring PCs, paper · LO 10
Goal: pairs design a structure that removes ambiguity and preserves history — and discover the disadvantages of folder copies themselves.
Show → Slide 5not spoken

Thandi's folders with dates and authors: Calculator/, Calculator_new/, Calculator (copy)/, Calculator_final/, Calculator_FINAL2/, calc_use_this/.

Say

This is Thandi's assessment folder. Same program, six folders. Work with the person next to you, on paper, Notes page Activity A. Three questions. One: which folder is the latest correct version, and what can't you tell from these names? Two: write down every disadvantage of keeping versions in separate folders. Three: design a better structure: one project, no ambiguity, and you must not lose the history. Six minutes.

Donot spoken

Pair people up. Anyone alone joins a pair. Walk the room; listen for "modified date" and "who changed it".

Waitnot spoken

Six minutes. At 1 minute left, say "one minute".

Ask the roomnot spoken
Pair at the back: which folder did you choose, and why can't you be sure? Second pair: what is your better structure?
Waitnot spoken

Take two pairs, maximum one minute each.

Say — answer

Here is what we can't tell from folder names: who made each one, when — the modified date changes when you copy a folder — why it was changed, and what exactly is different. Disadvantages of separate folders: duplicated files, wasted space, naming confusion, no author, no reason, hard to compare, and it is easy to submit or mark the wrong one.

The better design: one project folder with fixed, meaningful names that never change, plus a log of checkpoints: number, date, author and reason. Keep that idea, because a version control system is exactly that log, kept for you automatically.

Notenot spoken

Delegates will write their own answer to this problem into day-01/task1/README.md in Session 2B. That is their 2A evidence.

2A-4 · What a VCS is; trunk and branches

10:49–10:57 (8 min) · Slides 6–7 · Notes A4–A5 · LO 5, 7, 8, 9
Goal: define VCS, repository and commit; distinguish trunk/main from a branch; list advantages of branches.
Show → Slide 6not spoken

VCS: the robot librarian.

Say

Back to the six-year-old. Imagine the fridge has a robot librarian. Every time you say "save", it photographs every drawing on the fridge at once, writes the number, the time, your name and your reason on the back, and files the photos in a book it never loses.

That robot is a Version Control System, a VCS. The difference from ordinary revision control: it is automatic, it covers the whole project — all files together — and it can compare any two versions and take you back to any of them. The book of photos is the repository. One photo with its note is a commit.

Show → Slide 7not spoken

Trunk/main as the main road; a branch as a side road that rejoins.

Say

Now trunk and branch. The trunk, which Git calls main, is the main road: the version everybody trusts. A branch is a side road. You want to try a new idea without breaking the trusted version? Take a side road. If it works, the side road joins the main road again — that is a merge. If it fails, you just abandon the side road and main never knew.

Ask the roomnot spoken
Thumbs: you want to try a completely new way to calculate marks in a program that works. Main or a branch? Thumbs up for main, sideways for branch.
Waitnot spoken

Expect sideways thumbs.

Say — answer

Branch. Advantages of branches: experiments are safe, several people can work in parallel, you can review before merging, and you can throw failed ideas away. This week you will all work on main only — at Level 2, branches are a concept to explain, not a command to master. Level 4 creates and switches branches with commands.

2A-5 · Centralised versus distributed VCS

10:57–11:03 (6 min) · Slide 8 · Notes A6 · LO 11, 12
Goal: explain both models; know that Git is distributed; link it to Deep Freeze.
Show → Slide 8not spoken

One library book versus everyone holding a full copy.

Say

Centralised: there is one library with the only copy of the book and all its history. To read or write, you must go to the library. If the library is closed or burns down, nobody can work.

Distributed: everybody gets a full photocopy of the book, including all its history. You can work at home, offline, then meet up and combine. If one copy is lost, any other copy has everything.

Say

Git is distributed. GitHub is just a website that keeps one copy that everybody agrees to share. So Git is the tool, GitHub is a place. Not the same thing.

And here's why this matters to us this week. These lab PCs are frozen: tonight they forget everything you did today. But GitHub will remember. Tomorrow morning you clone, and your whole history comes back to the PC. Distributed version control is literally what saves your portfolio this week.

Ask the roomnot spoken
Quick check, hands up. One: Git and GitHub — same thing? Two: in a distributed VCS, where is the full history? Three: name the two main components of a revision.
Waitnot spoken

Answers: no; in every copy; timestamp and author.

2B-1 · The parcel to Granny: four places your work lives

11:40–11:48 (8 min) · Slide 12 · Notes B1
Goal: a mental model before any command: working folder → staging area → local commit → GitHub.
Show → Slide 12not spoken

The parcel: table, open box, sealed and labelled box, post office.

Say

Six-year-old version again. You want to send presents to Granny. First you put things on the table — that's your working folder, where you make and change files. Then you choose which things go into the box. Not everything on the table, only what Granny should get. That's the staging area, and the command is git add.

Then you close the box and write a label: what's inside and why. That's a commit, with its message. Last, you take the box to the post office. That's git push, and the post office is GitHub.

Ask the roomnot spoken
I've sealed the box and written the label. Is the parcel at Granny yet?
Waitnot spoken
Say — answer

No! A commit lives only on this PC. Only push takes it to GitHub. On a frozen PC, a commit you didn't push is gone tomorrow. Two more words: git status is looking at the table and the box — what changed, what's packed. git log is the list of sealed boxes you've already sent.

2B-4 · Good commit messages and file names

12:16–12:24 (8 min) · Slide 15 · Notes B6
Goal: delegates can tell a meaningful commit message from a useless one, and know the file-naming rules.
Say

The label on Granny's box. "Stuff" is a useless label. "Chocolate birthday cake, keep upright, open on the 12th" — Granny knows what it is, how to treat it and why it came. A commit message is the label on a revision. In six months, it is the only thing that tells you why something changed.

Show → Slide 15not spoken

Six messages: update · asdf · Day 1: Fix missing bracket in welcome.py · final · changes to stuff · Day 1: Add IPO chart for welcome program.

Ask the roomnot spoken
With your neighbour: which are good, and what makes them good? 60 seconds.
Waitnot spoken
Say — answer

The two good ones start with the day, use an action verb (Add, Fix, Update, Remove), say what, and are short enough to read in a list. One commit = one logical change. File names: lower case, no spaces, meaningful, never "final" or "new" — Git already knows which one is new.

2B-5 · Activity B: the messy status (session problem, independent)

12:24–12:48 (24 min) · Slide 16 · Notes Activity B · individual, neighbour checks

The four-step instructions for making the mess.

Now, on your own: you're going to make a realistic mess, and then clean it up like a professional. Four steps on the slide. A: add a second print line to hello.py and save. B: in the README, under "My answer to the folder-chaos problem", write your answer from the paper activity. C: make a private note file with something that must not be submitted. Type → Git Bashnot spoken

notepad day-01/task1/notes_to_self.txt
cp day-01/task1/hello.py day-01/task1/hello_backup.py

Say

Look at your git status. You should see two modified files and two untracked files. Your job: decide which belong in your portfolio, stage only those, check what's in the box, commit with a message that describes exactly what you did, and push. Then remove the two junk files. Twelve minutes. Notes Activity B has the questions.

Waitnot spoken

Walk the room. Ask individuals: "Why didn't you stage the backup?" Watch for git add . and git add day-01/task1/, both of which take the junk too.

Say — answer

Modified and wanted: hello.py and README.md. Untracked and not evidence: notes_to_self.txt (private) and hello_backup.py (Git is the backup). So we stage files one by one, not the whole folder:

Type → Git Bashnot spoken
git add day-01/task1/hello.py day-01/task1/README.md
git diff --cached --name-only
git commit -m "Day 1: Task 1 - add folder-chaos answer to README and second greeting to hello.py"
git push origin main
rm day-01/task1/notes_to_self.txt day-01/task1/hello_backup.py
git status
Say

Two rules come out of this. Normally you stage the whole task folder — that's what the Day 2 to 5 presenters will ask. But if there's junk in the folder, either delete it first or stage file by file. And always run git diff --cached --name-only before you commit: look in the box before you seal it.

Notenot spoken

If a delegate already committed the junk: git rm --cached day-01/task1/hello_backup.py, commit "Day 1: Remove backup file from Task 1", push. Never reset --hard or push --force.

Curriculum: Topic 2 (2.1.2 computational thinking, 2.1.3 PDLC, 2.1.5 Polya, 2.2 algorithms, IPO) and Topic 3 (block-based programming; compiler vs interpreter; shell vs IDE). Output: day-01/task2/welcome.py + algorithm.md, pushed.

P-1 · Unplugged: the robot that does exactly what you say

13:30–13:40 (10 min) · Slide 17 · whole room · Notes C1
Goal: everybody experiences why an algorithm must be precise, ordered and unambiguous.
Say

Wake-up exercise after lunch. I am now a robot. I do exactly what you tell me, nothing more, and I don't guess. My task: walk from here to that door and open it. Give me instructions, one at a time.

Donot spoken

Follow every instruction literally. "Walk to the door" → "Error: I don't know 'door'." "Walk forward" → walk until you bump the desk. "Open the door" while still 2 m away → mime grabbing air. Keep it to about 5 minutes and let them get you there.

Ask the roomnot spoken
What went wrong along the way? What did the robot need from you?
Waitnot spoken

Collect: exact steps, the right order, nothing missing, nothing ambiguous, a clear end.

Say — answer

That's the definition of an algorithm: a finite list of precise, unambiguous steps, in the right order, that solves a problem. A program is an algorithm written in a language the computer understands, and syntax is the grammar of that language. Your Level 2 learners will be in exactly the same position as you were: the computer is the robot.

P-2 · Computational thinking: the four pillars

13:40–13:52 (12 min) · Slide 17 · Notes C2 · pairs, paper · LO 2.1.2
Goal: name and apply decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design to the afternoon's session problem.
Show → Slide 17not spoken

The four pillars, each with a child's example.

Say

Computational thinking is thinking about a problem so that a computer, or a robot, could carry out the solution. Four pillars, each explained to a six-year-old.

Decomposition: "Tidy your room" is too big. Break it up: toys in the box, clothes in the cupboard, books on the shelf.

Pattern recognition: all socks go in the same drawer. When you've solved one sock, you've solved them all.

Abstraction: a taxi route map shows the stops, not every tree and pothole. Keep what matters, leave out the rest.

Algorithm: the recipe. The steps, in order.

Say

This afternoon's session problem: create a program that displays a learner's name, course level and a welcome message in a clear three-line format. With your neighbour, on paper, Notes C2: apply all four pillars to that problem. Four minutes.

Waitnot spoken
Say — answer

Decomposition: show the name; show the level; show the welcome. Pattern: all three are the same action, "display a line of text", so one instruction, used three times. Abstraction: we don't care about fonts, colours or which learner; just three lines of text. Algorithm: 1 display name, 2 display level, 3 display welcome, 4 stop.

P-3 · From problem to plan: Polya, PDLC, IPO

13:52–14:00 (8 min) · Slide 18 · Notes C3 · LO 2.1.3, 2.1.5, 2.2.6
Goal: place the program in the PDLC and draw its IPO chart. Day 2 goes deep into this; today is the overview only.
Show → Slide 18not spoken

Polya's four steps next to the PDLC; the IPO chart for the welcome program.

Say

George Polya gave us four steps for any problem: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back. The Program Development Life Cycle says the same thing in software words: analyse, design, code, test, then document and maintain. We did “understand” and “plan” with the pillars. Tomorrow's presenters take this much further.

Say

An IPO chart has three columns: Input, what comes in; Processing, what we do with it; Output, what goes out. For our program, there's no input yet, because the values are fixed in the code; processing is just putting the lines in the right order; output is three lines on the screen. A boring IPO chart, and that's fine: it's a first program.

P-5 · Interpreter vs compiler, shell vs IDE: a tour of Thonny

14:05–14:15 (10 min) · Slide 19 · Thonny · Notes C5 · Topic 3
Goal: distinguish compiler/interpreter and shell/IDE, and point at each part of Thonny.
Show → Slide 19not spoken

Translator analogy and the Thonny screen labelled.

Say

A compiler is like a translator who takes your whole book, translates all of it, and hands you a finished translated book. C++ works like that: you'll see it in Level 3. An interpreter is like a translator standing next to you at a meeting, translating one sentence at a time, as you speak. Python is interpreted.

Say

Open Thonny. The top part is the editor: you write a whole program and save it as a file. The bottom part is the shell, with three arrows: you type one line and Python answers immediately. Thonny itself, with editor, shell, run button and debugger together, is an IDE: an Integrated Development Environment. Your workshop.

Type → Thonny shell (bottom)not spoken

One line at a time, press Enter after each. Everybody types along.

2 + 3
print("Hello")
"Ha" * 3
Ask the roomnot spoken
Git Bash has a $ prompt. Thonny's shell has >>>. Both are shells. What's the difference?
Waitnot spoken
Say — answer

The $ shell talks to Windows and Git. The >>> shell talks to Python. If you type git status into Python, or print() into Git Bash, you get an error. Learners mix these up all the time, so show them the prompt.

Now we break it on purpose. On line 2, delete the closing quotation mark, just before the bracket. Run it.

Show → Thonnynot spoken

Read the message aloud: SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 2). Point at the line number and at the red highlight.

Say

Three things to read in every error message: which line, what kind of error, and the short explanation. Syntax error means the grammar is wrong, so Python refused to run any of it. Even line 1 didn't print. Fix it and run again.

Donot spoken

Second break, quickly: change print to Print on line 3 and run. Lines 1 and 2 do print, then: NameError: name 'Print' is not defined.

Ask the roomnot spoken
Why did lines 1 and 2 print this time, but not last time?
Waitnot spoken
Say — answer

The first was a syntax error: the grammar was broken, so nothing ran. The second is a runtime error: the grammar was fine, Python started running, and crashed when it reached line 3. Python is case-sensitive. Day 2 adds the third kind: logic errors, where it runs but gives the wrong answer.

Say

Cheat sheet: every term in one plain sentence
  • Revision = one saved, changed state of a document or program.
  • Revision number = the label that tells revisions apart (Git uses a short code like 3f2a9c1).
  • Timestamp / author = the two main components of a revision: when, and who. The message adds why.
  • Revision control = any method of keeping and organising revisions (even a paper log).
  • VCS = software that does revision control automatically for a whole project: records, compares, restores.
  • Repository = the project folder plus its complete history.
  • Commit = one checkpoint in the history: snapshot + author + timestamp + message.
  • Trunk / main = the trusted main line of development. Branch = a separate line for experiments; merge = joining it back.
  • Centralised VCS = one server holds the history; everyone must connect to it (e.g. Subversion).
  • Distributed VCS = every clone holds the full history (Git, Mercurial).
  • Git vs GitHub = tool vs website that hosts repositories.
  • Fork = your copy of someone's repo, on GitHub. Clone = a copy onto your PC. Push = send commits up. Pull = bring changes down.
  • Working folder / staging area / commit / push = table / box / sealed labelled box / post office.
  • Untracked (red, new to Git) · modified (red, changed since last commit) · staged (green, in the box).
  • Computational thinking = decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design.
  • Compiler = translates the whole program first (C++). Interpreter = translates and runs line by line (Python).
  • Shell = type one command, get an answer (>>> Python, $ Git Bash). IDE = editor + run + shell + debugger in one (Thonny).
  • Syntax error = broken grammar, nothing runs. Runtime error = crashes while running. Logic error = runs, wrong answer.
If stuck: fixes for what delegates will see
What the delegate seesWhat to do
"Windows protected your PC" when opening PortableGitMore info → Run anyway. If there's no Run anyway button, the PC blocks .exe files: use the USB extracted folder; if that also won't run, use the Codespaces plan (Backups).
Can't find git-bash.exeFile Explorer → Downloads → PortableGit → git-bash.exe. If the PortableGit folder isn't there, they never ran the download: double-click it.
Paste does nothing in Git BashRight-click → Paste, or Shift+Insert.
fatal: not a git repositoryWrong folder: cd ~/Documents/ncv-level2-python-submissions-2026, then pwd.
git remote -v shows fredreThey cloned the original: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/THEIR-USERNAME/ncv-level2-python-submissions-2026.git. If they haven't forked yet, fork first.
Repository not found on cloneTypo in username, or the fork doesn't exist yet. Copy the URL from the green Code button on their fork.
New folder doesn't appear in git statusIt's empty. Git only sees files.
Status says clean, but the file isn't on GitHubFile saved outside the repo (Desktop / Documents). Thonny: File → Save As into the task folder.
Author identity unknowngit config --global user.name "..." and user.email "...", then commit again. (Every morning after Deep Freeze.)
Push: no browser window, or asks for passwordNever type the password. Close Git Bash, reopen git-bash.exe from the PortableGit folder, push again; choose Sign in with your browser. Make sure the browser is signed in to their account, not a neighbour's.
GH007: Your push would publish a private email addressTheir GitHub hides their e-mail. In GitHub → Settings → Emails, copy the ...@users.noreply.github.com address; git config --global user.email "that-address"; git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit; push again.
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main'Committed but didn't push: git push origin main.
Permission denied (403) on pushPushing to someone else's repo (fredre or a neighbour). Check git remote -v. Signed in as the wrong user: Windows Credential Manager → Windows Credentials → remove git:https://github.com, push again.
Unwanted file stagedgit restore --staged FILE, then git diff --cached --name-only.
Unwanted file already committedgit rm --cached FILE, commit "Day 1: Remove ...", push.
Vim opened (screen full of ~)Type :wq and press Enter.
Account e-mail verification never arrivesCheck spam; resend; try a different e-mail. Meanwhile they follow along on a neighbour's screen and catch up in 2B-5.

Never tell anyone to use git push --force, git reset --hard, or to delete their fork.
